interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'll use a launch-timing disagreement, because it's a clean example of disagreeing without derailing the relationship.

Two weeks before a launch, I found an edge case affecting about 3% of users. My PM wanted to ship on schedule; I thought that gap was too risky to ship silently. Rather than just pushing back verbally, I put together the actual numbers — expected affected users, support ticket cost if it shipped broken, engineering cost of a two-day delay — and proposed a middle path: ship on time behind a feature flag, so we could roll back instantly if the edge case caused real damage.

The PM agreed once the trade-off was concrete rather than a gut feeling on either side. We shipped on schedule, the flag caught one bad interaction on day two, we fixed it in place, and the impact was contained to a few hours instead of the full user base.

What I'd emphasize if asked to go deeper: the disagreement didn't get resolved by one of us being more senior or more persuasive — it got resolved by turning a values disagreement (risk tolerance) into a data disagreement (expected cost), which is almost always more tractable.

**Testing:** whether you can disagree productively and land on a concrete resolution, rather than either capitulating immediately or digging in without offering an alternative.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Conflict

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide which story to tell when a question could fit several of your experiences?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I match on the competency being probed first, not the surface wording of the question — because most questions are one of a small set of underlying asks dressed differently.

Concretely, I keep my stories tagged by primary and secondary competency ahead of time (ownership, conflict, ambiguity, failure/growth, influence). When a question comes in, I ask myself what it's really testing — "tell me about a disagreement" and "tell me about a time you pushed back on a decision" are the same underlying ask — then I pull whichever tagged story is freshest and has the strongest numbers, not necessarily the first one that comes to mind.

If two stories fit equally well, I default to the one I haven't used yet in this loop, since repeating the same story to multiple interviewers who later compare notes can read as a thin bank even when each individual telling is honest.

One thing I actively avoid: forcing a story that's a weak fit just because it's the one I'm most comfortable telling. A weak fit shows up immediately in the follow-ups, because the details won't actually support the angle being asked about.

**Testing:** whether you have a deliberate retrieval process rather than defaulting to whichever anecdote is top-of-mind, which is what produces stories that don't quite answer the question asked.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Retrieval

interviewQuestions.question: Can you give me an example where you didn't have a clean win — a time it genuinely didn't go well?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes — I keep at least two real failure stories in my bank specifically because a bank of only wins reads as evasive, and this question comes up often enough that improvising it live is a bad bet.

One example: I owned a migration where I underestimated how much traffic a legacy endpoint still carried, based on stale internal docs instead of checking current metrics myself. We cut it over, broke a downstream integration nobody had flagged, and had a two-hour incident before we rolled back.

What actually failed was my process, not just bad luck: I trusted a doc instead of pulling live traffic data before a cutover with real blast radius. Afterward, I made pulling current metrics a required step in our own migration checklist, and it caught a similar stale-assumption case on the next team's migration six months later.

I'd rather tell this one than a softened version, because a real failure with a real fix is far more convincing than a story engineered to look modest while secretly flattering. Interviewers can usually tell the difference.

**Testing:** whether you have genuine self-reflection material ready, versus a fake-failure answer that's actually a disguised brag — covered in [red flags & common mistakes](behavioral-red-flags).
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Failure

interviewQuestions.question: How do you keep your story bank from going stale as you move into more senior roles?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat it as a living document, not a one-time prep artifact — refreshed roughly every 6-12 months and after any project that clearly produced new material.

The habit that makes this cheap: right after a notable incident at work — an outage, a hard conversation, a decision I made under ambiguity — I write two or three sentences into a running notes doc while it's fresh: what happened, what I specifically did, what the number was. Reconstructing that six months later from memory is much harder and usually loses the numbers first.

As I've moved to more senior scope, I've also had to retire some early-career stories that were true but no longer show the right scope — a story about fixing one bug well doesn't carry the same weight once I'm expected to show ownership across a whole system or team. So refreshing isn't just adding new stories; it's actively swapping out ones that no longer match the level I'm interviewing for. [Calibrating your answers to your level](behavioral-calibrating-level) covers how that scope shift should read in the actual answer.

**Testing:** whether you treat prep as an ongoing practice tied to your actual career progression, rather than a one-time exercise you did before your last job search.
